items.prompt: What happened to the liquid water in the puddle as the sun warmed it?
choices: It changed into tiny drops that floated up on the wind
It changed into water vapor, which is a gas
It changed into runoff and flowed downhill to a stream
It changed into cold air that rose high above the ground
items.why: The source says the sun's energy warmed the puddle and the liquid water slowly changed into a gas called water vapor. Vapor is a gas, not drops; the puddle's water evaporated rather than flowed away as runoff; water does not become air.

items.prompt: Which list names only kinds of precipitation?
choices: Rain, dust and hail
Snow, sleet and water vapor
Rain, clouds and sleet
Snow, sleet and hail
items.why: The source names rain, snow, sleet and hail as precipitation. Dust, water vapor and clouds are not water falling from clouds.

choices: The change from a gas to a liquid
The change from a liquid to a gas
The fall of water from clouds
The flow of water downhill over the ground
items.why: The source: this change from gas to liquid is called condensation. Liquid to gas is evaporation, falling water is precipitation, flowing water is runoff.

items.prompt: What is a cloud made of?
choices: Invisible water vapor rising with warm air
Billions of bits of dust held up by the cold air high above the ground
Billions of tiny drops of liquid water gathered around bits of dust
Heavy drops that are falling to the ground
items.why: The source: the drops gather around bits of dust, and billions of them together form a cloud. Vapor is invisible and not yet a cloud; the dust is only what the drops gather around, and it is the drops the air holds up; heavy falling drops are precipitation.

items.prompt: On a humid day, the outside of a cold glass gets wet. Which of these is the same change happening somewhere else in the water cycle?
choices: A puddle dries up on a warm, windy afternoon
Tiny drops bump into each other and join
Rain soaks into the soil, where roots take it in
Tiny drops form far up, where the air is colder than at the ground
items.why: Level 3 push: a new place for the unknown (the student must see what change the glass shows and find it again elsewhere, with no term named). The source: water vapor in the air touches the cold glass and turns to liquid, and high above the ground, where the air is colder, vapor cools and changes back into tiny drops. A drying puddle is the opposite change (liquid to gas); drops joining and rain soaking in are liquid water moving, with no change from gas to liquid.

items.prompt: Why do the drops in a cloud finally fall?
choices: They join and grow too heavy for the air to hold up
They cool and change from a gas into a liquid
They break apart into drops too small for the air to carry
They are warmed by the sun and evaporate
items.why: The source: the drops bump into each other and join, and when they grow too heavy for the air to hold up, they fall. Cooling into liquid is how the drops first form; the drops join, they do not break apart, and it is heavy drops that fall; being warmed and evaporating is how water leaves the ground, not why drops fall.

items.prompt: Rain lands on a hillside. Which two things does the passage say can happen to that water on the ground?
choices: It soaks into the soil or rises as tiny liquid drops
It rises as tiny liquid drops or cools into a gas
It soaks into the soil or runs downhill as runoff
It runs downhill as runoff or cools into a gas
items.why: The source: some water soaks into the soil, and some runs downhill over the surface as runoff. Water rises as vapor, not as drops; water becomes vapor when the sun warms it, not when it cools.

items.prompt: A student says, "The rain in each storm is brand-new water." Which idea from the passage best shows the student is wrong?
choices: Clouds make new drops to replace water that soaked into the soil
The rain is water that evaporated earlier and is now falling once more
Water that evaporates stays a gas, so it cannot fall again
Runoff that reaches a lake stays there and never evaporates again
items.why: Level 3 push: a reason to give, in a new place (the passage states the cycle from the puddle's side; the student must see what it means for rain). The source: the same water keeps moving through the steps, runoff evaporates again, and no new water is made. Clouds do not make new water; vapor does change back to liquid; water in lakes is warmed and evaporates again.

items.prompt: Two puddles are the same size and depth. Puddle 1 is in a town where the afternoon is warm and windy. Puddle 2 is in a town where it is cool and still. A student predicts both will be gone at the same time, because the same sun shines on both. What is wrong with the prediction?
choices: Evaporation is slower in cool, still air, so Puddle 2 lasts longer
Evaporation is slower in warm, windy air, so Puddle 1 will last longer
Evaporation stops when the air is still, so Puddle 2 never dries up
Nothing is wrong: the same sun dries both puddles at the same speed
items.why: Level 3 push: a reason to give (the student must judge a prediction and say which way the rule cuts). The source: evaporation happens faster when it is warm and windy, and slower when it is cool and still. Warm, windy air makes it faster, not slower; slower is not stopped, and the passage says the water evaporates sooner or later; the speed is not the same everywhere.

items.prompt: Water from a puddle ends up as part of a cloud. Which two changes did the water go through, in order?
choices: Condensation, then evaporation
Evaporation, then precipitation
Evaporation, then condensation
Runoff, then condensation
items.why: Level 3 push: an extra step (two changes of state to chain, with only the terms given and no clue words). The source: the puddle's liquid water changes to vapor (evaporation), the vapor rises, cools and changes back to tiny liquid drops (condensation), and those drops form the cloud. The reverse order would start with a gas; precipitation is water falling out of a cloud; runoff is water flowing downhill, not rising.
